overview: This sortie is the bridge from normal contact flying into engine and emergency-landing decision making. Be ready to brief the limits that matter, the PT6/PMU logic behind the indications you see, and the differences between an ELP, a PEL, and a forced landing when time and energy are running out.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Know the limits you are most likely to brief, violate, or use to decide whether the aircraft is still being flown normally. This is not a memorization contest for every number in NATOPS; it is about knowing the ones that change your go/no-go and landing decisions.

children.text: Maximum ramp weight is 6950 pounds. Maximum takeoff and landing weight are 6900 pounds. Maximum zero fuel weight is 5850 pounds.
Maximum baggage-compartment weight is 80 pounds.
Ground operation is limited to ambient temperatures from -23 C to +43 C.
Maximum touchdown rate is 600 FPM when the mains are serviced to 185 +/- 5 PSI, and 780 FPM when they are serviced to 225 +/- 5 PSI.
Those landing-rate numbers matter because a low-energy ELP or forced landing can tempt you into accepting a sink rate that damages the aircraft.
Do not open the canopy on the ground with surface winds above 40 knots.
Ejection-seat occupant limits are approximately 131.8 to 279.4 pounds including equipment and flight gear.

items.text: Use the Systems brief tool for the full NATOPS-style engine brief. For this event, be able to connect the PT6A-68, PMU, and propeller system to the cues that change whether you continue, PEL, force-land, or eject.

children.text: The PT6A-68 is a free-turbine engine, so the gas-generator section can still be healthy while the propeller side is the part misbehaving.
The PMU normally schedules fuel, acceleration, deceleration, and propeller response. Weight-on-wheels logic gives you about 60-61% N1 on the ground and about 67% N1 in flight.
The reduction gearbox and propeller interface logic are why NP, torque, and thrust can change even when the gas-generator section has not completely failed.
Healthy N1 with abnormal NP or torque should make you think propeller or control logic before you call it a total engine failure.
Loss of oil pressure or hydraulic pressure together with rapidly decaying N1, torque, and ITT is a much stronger engine-failure picture.
If the PMU drops offline or is selected OFF, fuel scheduling becomes manual and the workload jumps immediately, especially during landing or restart decisions.
Do not casually lift the PCL cutoff gate in flight. Mishaps have happened from inadvertent shutdown attempts.
Once ST READY extinguishes, the automatic start protections are gone, so any PMU OFF or manual-fuel work demands tighter monitoring.
Starts with PMU OFF are not recommended, and any event that leaves you in manual mode should immediately change how cautious you are with throttle movement and landing rollout planning.

items.text: Engine malfunctions are easier to manage when you stop chasing a single annunciator and instead build a full picture from power, N1, torque, ITT, NP, oil pressure, and hydraulic pressure.

children.text: A flameout usually gives you rapid loss of power and airspeed, rapidly decaying N1, torque, and ITT, loss of oil and hydraulic pressure, and the propeller moving toward feather.
An engine seizure can look similar, but often drives oil and hydraulic pressure to zero more abruptly and may include a CHIP warning.

A rollback is an uncommanded power reduction, often from PMU scheduling problems. If the PMU stays online, fuel flow and N1 may simply be lower than expected; if it drops offline, you may get a step change in power.
Uncommanded propeller feather usually shows up as reduced NP, increased torque, more prop noise, less thrust, and sometimes vibration.
A good quick discriminator is whether N1 is still healthy while torque or NP are not. That points you toward prop-system logic rather than a full engine failure.
High-value red warnings for this event are PMU FAIL, FUEL PX, OIL PX, CHIP, CHK ENG, GEN BUS, and BATT BUS.
PMU STATUS in flight matters because it can leave you at flight idle on landing and change the rollout picture.
Do not memorize every amber or white advisory for this event. Focus on the engine indications that change whether you continue, PEL, force-land, or eject.

items.text: The emergency landing pattern is the geometry you use for both a PEL and a forced landing. The profile is the same; the difference is whether power is still available and how you correct a low-energy state.

children.text: Interception is normally at high key, 3000 feet AGL, with 2500 feet AGL as the minimum high-key intercept.
Think of the profile in checkpoints: high key at 3000 feet AGL, low key at 1500 feet AGL, base key at 600-800 feet AGL, and final at 110 KIAS minimum.
Maintain 120 KIAS minimum until intercepting final. Do not trade airspeed away just to hit an altitude number.
Best glide clean is about 125 KIAS with roughly 1350-1500 FPM sink and about 2 nautical miles of glide for every 1000 feet lost.
With the gear down and clean otherwise, best glide is about 105 KIAS and glide ratio drops to about 1.6 nautical miles per 1000 feet lost.
Use winds, runway suitability, field elevation, and actual energy state to decide whether you can reach high key, low key, or need another option.

ORM 3-2-1 drives the low-altitude decision chain: do not descend below 2000 feet AGL in an actual forced-landing scenario unless you are on profile, runway in sight, and in a position to maneuver safely to land.
At 300 feet AGL you make the final continue-or-eject decision, at 200 feet the gear should be confirmed down, and at 100 feet the aircraft should be on centerline.
If the profile is falling apart, do not delay the wave-off in training or the eject decision in the real event.
A high-energy state is fixed with methods like 360s, bow ties, S-turns, slips, or early drag, but every choice should still preserve a predictable arrival at high key.
The primary reference in the ELP is the runway. Crosscheck actual position and energy against the next checkpoint early enough to make a smooth correction.
Do not descend below 2000 feet AGL in an actual forced-landing situation unless the runway is in sight, you are on profile, and you can still maneuver safely to land.
Allowing the aircraft to get slow to hit altitude checkpoints is dangerous; maintain 120 KIAS minimum until intercepting final and 110 KIAS minimum on final.
Treat ORM 3-2-1 and the final continue/eject gate as hard warning-and-caution discipline, not as flexible guidelines.

items.text: A PEL is for an engine problem where power still exists but failure may be imminent. The student trap is treating it like a routine recovery and burning up the engine's remaining time with slow procedures or excessive troubleshooting.

children.text: The memory aid is Turn, Climb/Accelerate, Clean, Check, BIP, Determine, Deliver, Reduce, Lower, Report.
Turn toward the nearest suitable field immediately. Then climb at 140 KIAS to DEGA or accelerate to build energy if a climb is not appropriate.
Clean the aircraft as soon as practical because extra drag kills climb and glide performance.
Check for secondary indications and use boost pump and ignition as required.
Do not blindly select boost pump or ignition on if an airstart would not be warranted after a failure, such as oil-system malfunction, chip light, fire light, or FOD.
Determine the runway before intercepting the profile and deliver the ISPI report early enough that everyone else understands your plan.
Reduce to 4-6% torque no sooner than DEGA.
Lower the gear no later than high key, fly 120 KIAS minimum on profile, lower flaps no sooner than low key, and use power immediately to fix a low-energy state.
Inside base key, use normal power corrections to ensure a safe and controlled landing instead of preserving some imaginary perfect emergency picture.
Time is the critical resource in many PELs. Do not turn an impending engine failure into an actual one by being slow.
On a PEL, never accept being below profile prior to the actual point on the ground. Power is available, so use it.
If a safe landing becomes unlikely, the answer is not to keep troubleshooting. Commit to the next safe option.

items.text: A forced landing is what happens when power is gone or insufficient for continued flight and the airplane has enough energy to reach a suitable hard-surface landing area. If that energy or runway picture is not there, the answer becomes eject, not hope.

children.text: The first memory items are Zoom/Glide 125 KIAS minimum, PCL OFF, intercept the ELP, and attempt an airstart only if warranted.
Do not attempt an airstart if the failure involves oil-system malfunction, chip light, fire light, or FOD.
If an airstart is not warranted, pull the firewall shutoff handle and commit to either the forced landing or ejection decision.
Use the nearest suitable hard-surface field of adequate length and align the aircraft with the landing direction as early as possible.
If you cannot reach high key, intercept the ELP at another point with the proper configuration and airspeed rather than stretching the glide into a bad setup.
At low key, use flaps only if energy supports it. If the airplane is not on profile approaching base key, eject in the real event or wave off in the simulated one.
Do not descend below 2000 feet AGL in an actual engine-failure case unless you are on profile, runway in sight, and in a position to maneuver to land.
Maintain 110 KIAS minimum on final until the landing transition. Anticipate a longer flare with 4-6% torque simulating a feathered prop.
If touchdown will occur past the first one-third of the runway in a simulated event, wave off. In the actual event, do not delay the eject decision once safe landing is unlikely.
Air-starts are not recommended below 2000 feet AGL because the primary task there is either safe recovery or ejection.
A flamed-out engine at 125 KIAS typically shows 0% indicated N1, torque near zero, and may still show a small residual oil-pressure indication.
Do not dissipate energy casually in a real forced landing. Use the time you have to build the safest runway plan possible.

items.text: Aldis lamp signals matter when the radios are gone and the tower still has to control you. The student value here is not just the colors; it is knowing how to acknowledge them and how they change your immediate action.

children.text: On the ground: steady green means cleared to take off, flashing green means cleared to taxi, steady red means stop, flashing red means taxi clear of runway, flashing white means return to starting point, and alternating red/green means exercise extreme caution.

In flight: steady green means cleared to land, flashing green means return for landing, steady red means give way and continue circling, flashing red means do not land, and alternating red/green means exercise extreme caution.
A red pyrotechnic signal in flight means do not land and wave off immediately regardless of previous instructions.
Acknowledge in daytime with aileron or rudder movement on the ground and wing rocking in the air.
At night, acknowledge by flashing aircraft lights.

studyNotes.summary: Know the limits, understand what the engine and PMU are telling you, and commit early to the right landing-option chain before a manageable malfunction turns into an actual engine-failure problem.

summary: NATOPS limits, PT6/PMU basics, and the ELP-to-PEL-to-forced-landing decision chain.

items.text: Start with the big picture, then walk the air path, then the fuel path, and only then talk about cockpit indications. That flow makes the brief sound like you understand the engine instead of reciting disconnected parts.

children.text: Purpose: convert fuel and air into shaft horsepower for the propeller while supplying the accessory and lubrication systems that keep the engine alive.
Architecture: free-turbine, reverse-flow engine with separate gas-generation and power sections.
Briefing payoff: once you understand where power is made and how the propeller is controlled, engine-failure indications make a lot more sense.

items.text: The PT6A-68 is a free-turbine turboprop flat-rated to produce 1100 shaft horsepower. It is a reverse-flow design with two independent sections.

children.text: Gas-generation section: four-stage axial compressor, single-stage centrifugal compressor, combustion chamber, and single-stage compressor turbine.
Power section: two-stage axial-flow power turbine, exhaust case, and reduction gearbox.
The power turbine is not mechanically linked to the compressor. That is why the engine can still be producing gas-generator indications even when the propeller side is degrading.
The reduction gearbox takes turbine speed of roughly 30,000 RPM down to about 2000 RPM at the Hartzell four-blade constant-speed propeller.
The engine is cooled and lubricated by a dedicated oil system, and the engine data manager monitors the operating parameters that drive the EICAS messages you brief.
The accessory-drive section powers the engine-driven components that keep the engine, oil, and propeller-control systems functioning.

items.text: The air molecule brief is the easiest way to explain how the PT6 makes power: trace the air from the intake to the exhaust and explain what each section is doing to it.

children.text: Inlet air travels rearward through the intake duct and inertial separator, which helps throw debris and moisture out of the airstream.
The air then moves forward through the four-stage axial compressor and the single-stage centrifugal compressor. The diffuser slows that flow and converts velocity into static pressure.
Diffused air passes through straightening vanes before it mixes with atomized fuel in the combustion chamber.
The expanding gas first drives the single-stage compressor turbine, which is mechanically linked to the compressor and keeps the gas-generator cycle going.
That same gas then drives the separate two-stage power turbine, which turns the reduction gearbox through its own shaft.
Exhaust gases leave through the stacks and add a small amount of thrust, but the real output the pilot cares about is the shaft power being delivered to the propeller.

items.text: The fuel molecule brief should explain how the engine meters fuel rather than just saying fuel goes to the nozzles.

children.text: Fuel leaves the tanks and reaches the engine fuel pump and fuel-management unit, where it is metered based on PCL position and system inputs.
Metered fuel is sent through the flow divider to the fuel nozzles, where it is atomized into the compressed air inside the combustion chamber.
During start, the igniters light the mixture. Once the engine is running, combustion becomes self-sustaining.
The PMU and related control logic are why fuel scheduling, acceleration, deceleration, and propeller response feel coordinated in normal operations.

Mounted around the reduction gearbox are the chip detector, PIU, torque probe, and PMA, which is why a gearbox or propeller-control problem can change what the fuel and power picture looks like from the cockpit.
If you can explain how the FMU, PMU, and propeller-control pieces interact, you are much better prepared to talk through rollback, feather, or PMU-related malfunctions.
